q: Which files are on the runner when the install stage of a pipeline starts?
options: Everything on your laptop, including files git has never seen
The files from the last deploy on the production server
Only the files that git has, with no node_modules
Nothing at all, not even the code
why: A pipeline runs on a clean machine, and the first stage gets the code from git. A file that exists only on your laptop is missing, so a 'works on my machine' mistake shows up in minutes. In my test, the same code printed a value on the laptop and Cannot find module on a clean checkout.

q: The test stage fails. What happens to the build, push and deploy stages, and which version is live?
options: They run anyway, and the new version goes live
They are skipped, and the old version stays live
They run, but the deploy is cancelled at the end
Only the deploy is skipped, the new image is still built
why: A failed stage stops the line. The stages after it never start, so nothing broken is built or deployed. In my run the script ended with exit code 1 and the live container still answered with the old version.

q: A pipeline goes green and then waits until a person clicks Deploy. Which practice is it?
options: Continuous delivery
Continuous integration
Continuous deployment
Blue green deployment
why: All three use the same pipeline and differ in where the robot stops. CI builds and tests every push. Delivery stops before production and waits for a person. Deployment has no click and goes live by itself, so it needs stronger tests and a fast way back.

q: A release passed every stage and went live, and now it is bad. What is the quickest safe way back?
options: Rebuild the old commit and wait for the tests
Deploy the tag latest again
Delete the pipeline and fix it by hand on the server
Deploy the previous artifact again, using its commit id tag
why: Build once, tag with the commit id, and keep the last few artifacts. A rollback is then a deploy of an older tag: no build and no tests. It took 1.7 s in my run. Latest is a poor choice because it can point to a different image over time.

q: You change one line in src/server.js and nothing else. What happens to the npm cache key, which is made from the operating system and the hash of the lockfile?
options: The key changes, so the cache is missed
The key is deleted from the store
The key stays the same, so the cache is reused
The key changes only on Mondays
why: The key depends on the lockfile only. The same lockfile gives the same key, so the files come from the cache (0.8 s against 2.4 s cold on my test app). If you add a library, the lockfile changes, so the key changes.

q: npm test fails on the runner, and the pipeline is green. What do you look for first?
options: A step that hides the failure, such as || true after the test command
A cache key that is too long
A runner that is too fast
A Docker image that is too big
why: Green with failing tests means a step swallows the failure. In my test, npm test followed by || true printed 'deploying to production' with a failing test, and the same script without || true stopped with exit code 1. In GitHub Actions, check continue-on-error as well.
